citations.original_sentence: In recent years, large language models (LLMs) such as GPT series \citep{brown2020gpt3} \citep{openai2023gpt4} have demonstrated strong natural-language understanding and generation capabilities relevant to QA.
citations.context: Automatic question answering (QA) systems aim to enable users to pose natural-language questions and receive accurate, concise answers from a computer system. From early rule-based expert systems to modern deep-learning architectures grounded in information retrieval and machine reading comprehension, QA has undergone a remarkable transformation. In recent years, large language models (LLMs) such as GPT series \citep{brown2020gpt3} \citep{openai2023gpt4} have demonstrated strong natural-language understanding and generation capabilities relevant to QA. Nevertheless, QA systems built on a single LLM agent continue to face fundamental limitations. \emph{First}, single agents are prone to hallucination, producing factually incorrect outputs with high confidence. \emph{Second}, finite context windows impede reliable reasoning over long documents or multi-hop inference chains. \emph{Third}, a single model may lack sufficient domain coverage for a query that requires several areas of expertise; combining perspectives is one possible response whose benefit requires task-level evaluation.

citations.context: At the same time, multi-agent collaborative paradigms have emerged, drawing theoretical inspiration from Minsky's ``Society of Mind'' \citep{minsky1988society} and the formal foundations of multi-agent systems \citep{wooldridge1995intelligent}. For example, influential frameworks such as AutoGen \citep{wu2024autogen} and MetaGPT \citep{hong2024metagpt} illustrate the emergence of explicit multi-agent coordination. Through role specialization, mutual debate \citep{du2024multiagent_debate}, and structured task decomposition, multi-agent systems can improve answer verification and task performance.

citations.original_sentence: For example, dense retrieval enables open-domain evidence access \citep{karpukhin2020dpr}, whereas RAG combines retrieved evidence with generative answering \citep{lewis2020rag}.
citations.context: Automatic question answering is a core branch of natural language processing (NLP) that interprets a user’s information need and generates an answer. Its major paradigms, including rule-based and knowledge-base QA, information-retrieval (IR) QA, machine reading comprehension (MRC), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and LLM-based agentic QA, have accumulated rather than supplanted one another. They differ in their primary evidence sources, reasoning interfaces, and operational assumptions. For example, dense retrieval enables open-domain evidence access \citep{karpukhin2020dpr}, whereas RAG combines retrieved evidence with generative answering \citep{lewis2020rag}. Multi-agent systems introduce an explicit coordination layer when a task demands distributed retrieval, reasoning, verification, or tool use. Accordingly, the historical overview in this section should be regarded as a collection of representative milestones, rather than a single linear sequence of superseded paradigms. QA has also expanded from single-turn, closed-domain scenarios to multi-turn and open-domain settings. Benchmark datasets have been instrumental in driving research progress. Representative examples include HotpotQA \citep{yang2018hotpotqa} for multi-hop reasoning, Natural Questions \citep{kwiatkowski2019natural_questions} derived from real search queries, and CoQA \citep{reddy2019coqa} and QuAC \citep{choi2018quac} for conversational QA. These resources have facilitated advances in retrieval, generation, and complex reasoning. The representative milestones are illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:qa_timeline}.

citations.context: Automatic question answering is a core branch of natural language processing (NLP) that interprets a user’s information need and generates an answer. Its major paradigms, including rule-based and knowledge-base QA, information-retrieval (IR) QA, machine reading comprehension (MRC), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and LLM-based agentic QA, have accumulated rather than supplanted one another. They differ in their primary evidence sources, reasoning interfaces, and operational assumptions. For example, dense retrieval enables open-domain evidence access \citep{karpukhin2020dpr}, whereas RAG combines retrieved evidence with generative answering \citep{lewis2020rag}. Multi-agent systems introduce an explicit coordination layer when a task demands distributed retrieval, reasoning, verification, or tool use. Accordingly, the historical overview in this section should be regarded as a collection of representative milestones, rather than a single linear sequence of superseded paradigms. QA has also expanded from single-turn, closed-domain scenarios to multi-turn and open-domain settings. Benchmark datasets have been instrumental in driving research progress. Representative examples include HotpotQA \citep{yang2018hotpotqa} for multi-hop reasoning, Natural Questions \citep{kwiatkowski2019natural_questions} derived from real search queries, and CoQA \citep{reddy2019coqa} and QuAC \citep{choi2018quac} for conversational QA. These resources have facilitated advances in retrieval, generation, and complex reasoning. The representative milestones are illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:qa_timeline}.

citations.original_sentence: For instance, ReAct specifically interleaves reasoning and action \citep{yao2023react}.
citations.context: An LLM-based agent takes a large language model as its cognitive core and may be equipped with perception and action capabilities. For the analytical purposes of this review, we characterize agent functionality via four capabilities: \emph{Perception} (receiving environmental input), \emph{Planning} (task decomposition and goal setting), \emph{Action} (tool invocation and external interaction), and \emph{Memory} (short-term context management and long-term knowledge retrieval). This constitutes an analytical framework, rather than implying that every agent system implements these four identical components. For instance, ReAct specifically interleaves reasoning and action \citep{yao2023react}. Formally, a multi-agent collaborative QA system can be defined as: \begin{equation} \mathcal{S} = \langle \mathcal{A},\; \mathcal{C},\; \mathcal{T},\; \mathcal{E} \rangle \label{eq:mas_def} \end{equation} \noindent where $\mathcal{A} = \{a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_N\}$ is the set of agents with each $a_i = \langle \pi_i, \mathcal{M}_i, \mathcal{K}_i \rangle$ denoting its planning policy, memory state, and knowledge base; $\mathcal{C}$ is the communication protocol; $\mathcal{T}$ is the task space; and $\mathcal{E}$ is the shared execution environment.

citations.original_sentence: Representative milestones include the Transformer \citep{vaswani2017attention}, which introduced an attention-only sequence-transduction architecture; BERT \citep{devlin2019bert}, which advanced bidirectional pretraining and task-specific fine-tuning; and GPT-3 \citep{brown2020gpt3} and GPT-4 \citep{openai2023gpt4}, which demonstrated powerful few-shot and zero-shot capabilities.
citations.context: The trajectory of LLM development has been decisive in enabling this architecture. Representative milestones include the Transformer \citep{vaswani2017attention}, which introduced an attention-only sequence-transduction architecture; BERT \citep{devlin2019bert}, which advanced bidirectional pretraining and task-specific fine-tuning; and GPT-3 \citep{brown2020gpt3} and GPT-4 \citep{openai2023gpt4}, which demonstrated powerful few-shot and zero-shot capabilities. Open-weight releases such as LLaMA \citep{touvron2023llama} and ChatGLM \citep{glm2024chatglm} provide additional options for local experimentation, while InstructGPT \citep{ouyang2022instructgpt} exemplifies the use of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) to improve instruction following. Table~\ref{tab:llm_evolution} summarizes representative model capabilities relevant to agentic QA; this table serves as an illustrative overview rather than an exhaustive chronological record.

audit_history.original_sentence: Representative milestones include the Transformer \citep{vaswani2017attention}, which introduced self-attention; BERT \citep{devlin2019bert}, which established the pre-train--fine-tune paradigm; and GPT-3 \citep{brown2020gpt3} and GPT-4 \citep{openai2023gpt4}, which demonstrated powerful few-shot and zero-shot capabilities.
audit_history.context: The trajectory of LLM development has been decisive in enabling this architecture. Representative milestones include the Transformer \citep{vaswani2017attention}, which introduced self-attention; BERT \citep{devlin2019bert}, which established the pre-train--fine-tune paradigm; and GPT-3 \citep{brown2020gpt3} and GPT-4 \citep{openai2023gpt4}, which demonstrated powerful few-shot and zero-shot capabilities. Open-source models such as LLaMA \citep{touvron2023llama} and ChatGLM \citep{glm2024chatglm} further democratized agent development, while InstructGPT \citep{ouyang2022instructgpt} exemplifies the use of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) to improve instruction following. Table~\ref{tab:llm_evolution} summarizes representative model capabilities relevant to agentic QA; this table serves as an illustrative overview rather than an exhaustive chronological record.

citations.original_sentence: Inspired by Minsky's Society of Mind \citep{minsky1988society}, multi-agent architectures can combine agents with individual memory, reflection, and planning, as illustrated in social simulations \citep{park2023generative_agents}.
citations.context: The motivation for multi-agent systems is therefore capability extension rather than simple replacement. Inspired by Minsky's Society of Mind \citep{minsky1988society}, multi-agent architectures can combine agents with individual memory, reflection, and planning, as illustrated in social simulations \citep{park2023generative_agents}. A single ``generalist'' workflow may combine query understanding, retrieval, generation, and refinement, whereas a multi-agent workflow can separate these functions into, for example, Planner, Retriever, Generator, and Critic roles. MetaGPT demonstrates role allocation among product managers, architects, and engineers in software development \citep{hong2024metagpt}, while CAMEL studies sustained interaction between user and assistant roles \citep{li2023camel}. These examples show how role conditioning can structure collaboration, but they do not establish a universal advantage: specialization is useful only when roles have genuinely different information, tools, or verification responsibilities.

citations.original_sentence: For example, \citet{du2024multiagent_debate} report improved factuality and reasoning performance on the tasks they evaluate, whereas divergent prompting can mitigate convergence toward similar reasoning paths \citep{liang2024divergent_debate}.
citations.context: In the multi-agent debate paradigm, several LLM agents generate candidate answers and critique one another across one or more rounds. Representative studies illustrate both the potential and the limits of this design. For example, \citet{du2024multiagent_debate} report improved factuality and reasoning performance on the tasks they evaluate, whereas divergent prompting can mitigate convergence toward similar reasoning paths \citep{liang2024divergent_debate}. ReConcile provides another example by integrating heterogeneous models with confidence-weighted consensus \citep{chen2024reconcile}; inter-model inconsistency and capability imbalance nevertheless remain important considerations \citep{xiong2023inter_consistency}. Accordingly, adding more agents or debate rounds does not reliably boost QA performance; instead, the interaction rules, diversity of evidence, and aggregation procedure determine whether disagreement yields correction, inconsistency, or unnecessary computational cost.

citations.original_sentence: Selection should reflect the need for traceability, the availability of shared state, and the expected interaction cost \citep{wu2024autogen,qian2023chatdev,anthropic2024mcp,google2025a2a}.
citations.context: Explicit messaging makes the content and provenance of an agent's contribution inspectable, and is useful when agents must exchange evidence, explain decisions, or coordinate across distinct roles. Its main cost is message volume: repeated dialogue consumes context and adds latency, particularly as the team grows. Implicit communication reduces direct message passing by using shared environmental state, but it depends on agents being able to observe and interpret that state consistently; otherwise, changes may be ambiguous or difficult to audit. Standardized protocols address a different problem. MCP and A2A aim to improve interoperability between tools, data sources, and agents, but protocol compatibility alone does not guarantee useful coordination or reliable QA. Thus, explicit and implicit communication are interaction mechanisms, whereas protocols provide an interface layer that may support either. citations.original_sentence: Least-to-Most, Decomposed Prompting, and Plan-and-Solve primarily inform the first decision, whereas role profiles in MetaGPT and AgentVerse address the second \citep{zhou2023least_to_most,khot2023decomposed_prompting, wang2023plan_and_solve,hong2024metagpt,chen2024agentverse}.
citations.context: Decomposition, assignment, and orchestration solve related but distinct problems. Decomposition determines which sub-questions must be answered and how they depend on one another; assignment matches those sub-questions to agents; orchestration determines their execution order and whether the workflow should adapt at runtime. Least-to-Most, Decomposed Prompting, and Plan-and-Solve primarily inform the first decision, whereas role profiles in MetaGPT and AgentVerse address the second \citep{zhou2023least_to_most,khot2023decomposed_prompting, wang2023plan_and_solve,hong2024metagpt,chen2024agentverse}. A fixed sequence is adequate when dependencies and agent capabilities are known in advance; dynamic routing may be more suitable when query difficulty or available expertise varies, but it adds scheduling overhead and failure points. In either case, decomposition errors can propagate: omitted sub-questions leave gaps in the final answer, while unnecessary decomposition creates redundant calls and aggregation work. Pipeline-optimization tools such as DSPy can improve task-metric performance of language-model modules, but should not be treated as evidence that runtime recruitment or load balancing is effective \citep{khattab2024dspy}. Evaluation should distinguish decomposition quality, assignment fit, and orchestration efficiency rather than attributing an end-to-end gain to a single mechanism.

citations.original_sentence: Vector retrieval is one way to access such information: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) \citep{lewis2020rag,gao2024rag_survey} augments generation with retrieved documents.
citations.context: Long-term memory can retain historical experiences and domain knowledge in external stores \citep{zhang2024memory_survey}. Vector retrieval is one way to access such information: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) \citep{lewis2020rag,gao2024rag_survey} augments generation with retrieved documents. As one illustrative multi-agent implementation, a retrieval agent can select the Top-$k$ relevant documents from knowledge base $\mathcal{D}$ using cosine similarity: \begin{equation} \operatorname{Rel}(q,d_i) = \frac{\boldsymbol{\phi}(q)^{\top}\boldsymbol{\phi}(d_i)} {\|\boldsymbol{\phi}(q)\|\,\|\boldsymbol{\phi}(d_i)\|},\qquad \hat{\mathcal{D}} = \operatorname*{Top\text{-}k}_{d_i\in\mathcal{D}}\operatorname{Rel}(q,d_i) \label{eq:rag} \end{equation} where $\boldsymbol{\phi}(\cdot)$ is the dense encoder embedding function and $\hat{\mathcal{D}}$ is the set of retrieved relevant documents. Retrieval has evolved from passive retrieval to active variants. Self-RAG \citep{asai2024selfrag} uses reflection tokens to decide when to retrieve and to critique generated passages, while FLARE \citep{jiang2023active_rag} triggers retrieval when predicted upcoming text contains low-confidence tokens and then regenerates that text. These controls can inform retrieval components in a multi-agent workflow.

audit_history.original_sentence: A representative access mechanism is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) \citep{lewis2020rag,gao2024rag_survey}, through which multi-agent QA systems access long-term memory.
audit_history.context: Long-term memory typically relies on vector databases to store vast historical experiences and external domain knowledge \citep{zhang2024memory_survey}. A representative access mechanism is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) \citep{lewis2020rag,gao2024rag_survey}, through which multi-agent QA systems access long-term memory. A retrieval agent selects the Top-$k$ relevant documents from knowledge base $\mathcal{D}$ using cosine similarity: \begin{equation} \operatorname{Rel}(q,d_i) = \frac{\boldsymbol{\phi}(q)^{\top}\boldsymbol{\phi}(d_i)} {\|\boldsymbol{\phi}(q)\|\,\|\boldsymbol{\phi}(d_i)\|},\qquad \hat{\mathcal{D}} = \operatorname*{Top\text{-}k}_{d_i\in\mathcal{D}}\operatorname{Rel}(q,d_i) \label{eq:rag} \end{equation} where $\boldsymbol{\phi}(\cdot)$ is the dense encoder embedding function and $\hat{\mathcal{D}}$ is the set of retrieved relevant documents. Retrieval has evolved from early passive Naive RAG to active variants. For example, Self-RAG \citep{asai2024selfrag} and proactive retrieval (FLARE) \citep{jiang2023active_rag} allow specialised retrieval agents to autonomously determine when to retrieve, evaluate retrieval quality, and pass refined knowledge to the generation agent.

stage2_prior_context.original_sentence: Vector retrieval is one way to access such information: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) \citep{lewis2020rag,gao2024rag_survey} augments generation with retrieved documents.
stage2_prior_context.context: Long-term memory can retain historical experiences and domain knowledge in external stores \citep{zhang2024memory_survey}. Vector retrieval is one way to access such information: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) \citep{lewis2020rag,gao2024rag_survey} augments generation with retrieved documents. As one illustrative multi-agent implementation, a retrieval agent can select the Top-$k$ relevant documents from knowledge base $\mathcal{D}$ using cosine similarity: \begin{equation} \operatorname{Rel}(q,d_i) = \frac{\boldsymbol{\phi}(q)^{\top}\boldsymbol{\phi}(d_i)} {\|\boldsymbol{\phi}(q)\|\,\|\boldsymbol{\phi}(d_i)\|},\qquad \hat{\mathcal{D}} = \operatorname*{Top\text{-}k}_{d_i\in\mathcal{D}}\operatorname{Rel}(q,d_i) \label{eq:rag} \end{equation} where $\boldsymbol{\phi}(\cdot)$ is the dense encoder embedding function and $\hat{\mathcal{D}}$ is the set of retrieved relevant documents. Retrieval has evolved from passive retrieval to active variants. Self-RAG \citep{asai2024selfrag} uses reflection tokens to decide when to retrieve and to critique generated passages, while FLARE \citep{jiang2023active_rag} triggers retrieval when predicted upcoming text contains low-confidence tokens and then regenerates that text. These controls can inform retrieval components in a multi-agent workflow.

citations.original_sentence: Self-consistency and debate broaden the set of candidate reasoning paths; Chain-of-Agents distributes evidence processing across long inputs; reflection and critique revisit a provisional answer to identify and repair errors \citep{wang2023self_consistency,du2024multiagent_debate, zhang2024chain_agents,shinn2023reflexion,madaan2023self_refine, dhuliawala2023chain_of_verification}.
citations.context: These techniques seek reliability through different mechanisms. Self-consistency and debate broaden the set of candidate reasoning paths; Chain-of-Agents distributes evidence processing across long inputs; reflection and critique revisit a provisional answer to identify and repair errors \citep{wang2023self_consistency,du2024multiagent_debate, zhang2024chain_agents,shinn2023reflexion,madaan2023self_refine, dhuliawala2023chain_of_verification}. They are not interchangeable: sampling more paths helps only when those paths provide meaningful diversity, sequential evidence transfer can lose information, and a critic may share the generator's blind spots. Combining mechanisms is possible, but each extra pass adds inference cost and requires an aggregation or stopping rule. The appropriate choice therefore depends on the dominant failure mode: ambiguity among plausible answers, limited capacity to process long evidence, or the need to audit a provisional response. Reliability should be evaluated against these failure modes rather than inferred from the number of agents or reasoning rounds.

citations.original_sentence: Figure~\ref{fig:platform_resource_map} illustrates this layer with AutoGen, CrewAI, and MetaGPT \citep{wu2024autogen,crewai2023,hong2024metagpt}.
citations.context: The orchestration layer determines how agents are defined, assigned work, and coordinated during execution. Figure~\ref{fig:platform_resource_map} illustrates this layer with AutoGen, CrewAI, and MetaGPT \citep{wu2024autogen,crewai2023,hong2024metagpt}. Across the wider set of resources, some frameworks encode collaboration through predefined roles and procedures: for example, CAMEL uses role-conditioned dialogue, while ChatDev and MetaGPT organize work through staged, role-based processes \citep{li2023camel,qian2023chatdev,hong2024metagpt}. Other frameworks expose more control flow to developers: AutoGen supports configurable conversations, LangGraph represents workflows as state graphs, and AgentVerse provides a phased collaboration process \citep{wu2024autogen,duan2024langgraph_crewai, chen2024agentverse}. GPTSwarm explores optimization of agent connections. DSPy, by contrast, focuses on metric-driven optimization of language-model pipelines and is therefore an adjacent toolkit, not a like-for-like multi-agent framework \citep{zhuge2024gptswarm,khattab2024dspy}.

citations.context: Representative conventional benchmarks cover distinct answer-level capabilities. HotpotQA provides Wikipedia-based multi-hop questions with sentence-level supporting facts, making it appropriate for evaluating evidence-grounded retrieval and reasoning \citep{yang2018hotpotqa}. CoQA evaluates context-dependent conversational QA through connected question--answer turns \citep{reddy2019coqa}. MMLU tests broad multi-task knowledge and reasoning across academic subjects \citep{hendrycks2021mmlu}, whereas MuSiQue constructs multi-hop questions from single-hop components to probe connected reasoning \citep{trivedi2022musique}. audit_history.original_sentence: Conventional benchmarks and agent environments measure answer correctness or task completion \citep{hendrycks2021mmlu,yang2018hotpotqa, liu2024agentbench,mialon2024gaia}; they do not reveal whether debate added independent evidence, whether a long-context chain lost a decisive fact, or whether a critic detected and corrected an error.
audit_history.context: Section~4.5 covers diverse reasoning paths, sequential evidence processing, reflection, and mutual critique. These mechanisms address different failure modes, yet they are often compared only by final-answer accuracy. Conventional benchmarks and agent environments measure answer correctness or task completion \citep{hendrycks2021mmlu,yang2018hotpotqa, liu2024agentbench,mialon2024gaia}; they do not reveal whether debate added independent evidence, whether a long-context chain lost a decisive fact, or whether a critic detected and corrected an error. Additional reasoning rounds can also repeat the same assumptions or share correlated blind spots. Trace analyses such as MAST identify design, alignment, and verification failures \citep{han2024mast}, but process-level measures of contribution, complementarity, and error correction are not standard in QA evaluation.
